title: CRI and networking behavior
body:
### What happened?

This is a follow up to [this Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09QYUH5W/p1740368655309169). I can't say that I understand why, but I'm told this behavior is unexpected: the container runtime sometimes gets a `RunPodSandboxRequest` where the host port is zero.

### What did you expect to happen?

I believe @aojea wants to "check if we are sending that info on purpose through the CRI API or is just an oversight".

I think more importantly, the CRI is a bit under-documented here. The [documentation of `host_port`](https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/v0.32.2/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto#L204) is just `Port number on the host. Default: 0 (not specified)`, which reveals basically nothing about how an implementation might handle a zero value for that field.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This can be reproduced with minikube, Istio, and the Gateway API. It can probably be reproduced in other ways, too, but this is the most straightforward I came up with:

```bash
cd minikube  # https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube
git checkout v1.35.0
# Apply this 1-line patch so we can see `PodConfig` in the logs:
git apply patch
make local-kicbase-debug && make

# The problem can be illustrated most easily by booting up Istio and using the Gateway API
# (not sure why), but I was also observing host_port = 0 for my application pods.
./out/minikube start --container-runtime=containerd --memory=16384 --cpus=4
istioctl install --set profile=ambient --skip-confirmation
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.0/standard-install.yaml
```

Where `patch` is this:

```diff
diff --git a/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml b/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
index 873cee549..8bc7bf048 100644
--- a/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
+++ b/deploy/kicbase/containerd.toml
@@ -15,7 +15,7 @@ oom_score = 0
   address = ""
   uid = 0
   gid = 0
-  level = ""
+  level = "debug"

 [metrics]
   address = ""
```

Once you run the above, you can check the log by running:

```bash
docker exec -it minikube journalctl -u containerd | grep 'Sandbox config' | grep HostPort
```

You can see that a bunch of pods are run with a port mapping where `HostPort` is zero.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

/sig network

For reference, some detail of the process from one of my [presentations about kubernetes networking](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/14xNjy9ej8kGLkmSC7RsDO9-039vrwmf6sMofVOkqcD8/edit?usp=sharing)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/fade9f97-56ab-47ae-8e22-ea4907a1da91)

This is the method that calls the runtime from kubelet

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/staging/src/k8s.io/cri-client/pkg/remote_runtime.go#L190-L205

That is called from 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L40-L42

The Pod config is generated here

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L80

and port maps are added here to the config we send to the runtimes

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L117-L137

No place take into consideration that the HostPort is zero

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a18b4a8d97151a25c4d8088839d77e6ba482cac3/pkg/kubelet/container/helpers.go#L359-L395

So, this confirms we send to the CRI all the container ports information, but it seems we don't tell them what they are supposed to do if hostPort is zero

At first sight it seems a very impactful to stop sending the information:
- we must understand how CRIO (@mrunalp ) and Containerd (@MikeZappa87 ) are interpreting this information
- is there any other intention for these fields than implementing HostPorts on containers ( @thockin  may remember)
of course host port zero is invalid.. typically used by client tools to request an unused port number ...

Ok, cri-o also filters hostPort 0

https://github.com/cri-o/cri-o/blob/5991aec3baf922445791cb6dbb9ed4522e251c16/server/sandbox_run.go#L73-L88

I think now is safe to say that container runtimes should not do anything if hostPort <= 0, so we need to update the API docs

Do we feel we should also filter them in the kubelet side?
I think is better to leave it as is today, there is more information related to container ports there and since this was this way for so long, based on [Hyrum's Law](https://www.hyrumslaw.com/) someone may depend on it these days

I think it would be an api decision if they want to support dynamically assigning a port number each time.. and adding that dynamically assigned port to the port mappings.. but that would require some way to get an assignment and have it mapped through.. maybe an NRI plugin.

nod on the backwards compat versioning issues.. This is the way we deal with it today.. we ignore it. I'd bet if you look through you'll see we ignore it to maintain backwards compatibility with old specs..

Agree - 0 must be interpreted as "none" and not "dynamic".  Realisitically, this should never have been sent to CRI if the value is 0 ("not specified") but it was.  We don't have any real plans for randomly-allocated hostports, but if we did it would need to be something other than "hostPort = 0"
So waht is the AI for this issue and who is on it?

Talked about this in the SIG Network meeting:

Originally it should have been an optional field (e.g. pointer in Go), but at this point we can't change that without breaking things. The expectation from hereon is that you have to "ignore 0".

Code Links: [1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9fe95e7586c8778d3b33737a48b7fbf7fa6416f9/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_sandbox.go#L123), [2](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/79309361be72cb679cb46bcb863a2d9b15dfe707/internal/cri/server/sandbox_run.go#L441), [3](https://github.com/kubernetes/cri-api/blob/3dd84b8b2b65ecdf2087863f2e028266cfa46dcb/pkg/apis/runtime/v1/api.proto#L205), [4](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/79309361be72cb679cb46bcb863a2d9b15dfe707/internal/cri/server/sandbox_run.go#L509)

The thing to do here is improve our documentation. We should improve the api.proto documentation for this:

> We don't have any real plans for randomly-allocated hostports, but if we did it would need to be something other than "hostPort = 0"

Really? AFAIK opening a socket with the port set to 0 is the only reliably way to get a randomly allocated port? This tells the OS you don't care and the OS is the only one that can find an open port without a race.

That ... actually seems like the correct way to ask for a random port.
Doesn't matter whether it makes sense -- using 0 to mean "not specified" dates all the way back.

title: CEL,CRD: Combining nested macros and CIDR containing another CIDR checks doesnt seem to work
body:
### What happened?

Hi, I trying to use CEL validation on a CRD to verify a given subnet from one field is in range of subnets of another field, but it doesnt seem to work. Please see bellow details: 

The CRD has the following fields
```
subnets:
  description: ...
  items:
    maxLength: 43
    type: string
    x-kubernetes-validations:
    - message: CIDR is invalid
      rule: isCIDR(self)
  maxItems: 2
  minItems: 1
  type: array
  x-kubernetes-validations:
  - message: When 2 CIDRs are set, they must be from different
      IP families
    rule: size(self) != 2 || !isCIDR(self[0]) || !isCIDR(self[1])
      || cidr(self[0]).ip().family() != cidr(self[1]).ip().family()
excludeSubnets:
  description: ...
  items:
    maxLength: 43
    type: string
    x-kubernetes-validations:
    - message: CIDR is invalid
      rule: isCIDR(self)
  maxItems: 25
  minItems: 1
  type: array
```

Using the following rule, to verify each item in `excludeSubnets` is in range of at least one item in `subents`:
```
self.excludeSubnets.all(e, self.subnets.exists(s,cidr(s).containsCIDR(cidr(e))))
```
1. Given the following input the validation should block the request (return false): 
```
subnets: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
excludeSubnets: ["192.200.0.0/30", "192.300.0.1/32"]
```
2. Given the following input the validation should pass (return true): 
```
subnets: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
excludeSubnets: ["192.168.0.100/32", "192.168.0.1/32"]
```
The rule doesnt seem to work and result in blocking inputs (i.e.: return false in both cases).




### What did you expect to happen?

I expect the above CEL rule to work, it should return false for input (1), and return true for input (2).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Install the following CRD  [crd.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18981991/crd.md)
Apply [cudn-should-fail.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18985446/cudn-should-fail.md), expect failure.
Apply [cudn-should-pass.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18981992/cudn-should-pass.md), expect success.

### Anything else we need to know?

It seem that nested macros work with more simple condition, please see this [CEL playground example](https://playcel.undistro.io/?content=H4sIAAAAAAAAA3WS22rCQBCGX2WaXqgQDy30RnojRWiLbaVSpJCbMRnjwmY37OxqpPTdOxsDYkECYTKH%2F%2FtnNz9JTjqZJuMxrEnntiLwFvyO4Gm%2BgKXGY%2BlsMMVNZqTlMgeKAQ0o48lh7tWeRGMzY6Zqo49Q2wM5KoDMXjlrKjI%2BalNTa%2BtIJosYk1Nt5aD87sS1VWUNzJvaEbOScIGmDFgS9IU%2FGEUnrZshrJ3yBEcbXGuNzjM7QXdNX0ytMDpCkFKMWRUEW%2BvEfB08FOgxlRi%2BZ28LkPTr6uM91iv0ncoyKkPvM5heu8UedcArcCxRGfYt6QzohObd%2FnEut1qTnJzM2K0oYFVr4s4Y18phrGXyUJPrUNAqbAx5HqHWfUqBu09qFHvucwoEj8AwGGQmSZNIfYl8ueBbeJYjiVd26erK1qMI7eSnmRnC3WTy30Wbf5icqvF9H3uEW9mCBBn%2FrN8%2FNsGsyWECAAA%3D)

I've set up an example of this in the openshift API examples (we use this to test patterns), and as far as I can tell this does work, see the way I've implemented this here https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2213

It's largely the same as your description but I had to change the `self.excludeSubnets.all(e, self.subnets.exists(s,cidr(s).containsCIDR(cidr(e))))` rule slightly to account for when `excludeSubnets` is not present

On further discussion, it appears that there's a bug here

The CIDR check works correctly when the IP addresses are the same (`192.168.0.0/16` will contain `192.168.0.0/24`) but when the IP addresses are not equal, this doesn't work. The part of the code that's supposed to mask the address based on the number of bits, doesn't actually do what was intended.

/cc @cici37 can you take a look? Thanks!

/triage accepted
Thank you so much for the quick fix!

nodes.title: Fix implementation of ContainsCIDR to allow non-equal addresses
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The implementation of `containsCIDR` was supposed to compare masked IP addresses. If the second IP address is masked to the same number of bits as the first, and they are equal, then the second IP address must be within the first subnet, assuming the subnet prefix length is less or equal.

The second half of the assertion for `equalMasked` was not actually masking the address, and therefore if the IPs weren't exactly equal, we would reject otherwise valid CIDR inclusions.

Eg

```
cidr('192.168.0.0/16').containsCIDR('192.168.0.0/32') <- This works today
cidr('192.168.0.0/16').containsCIDR('192.168.0.1/32') <- This does not work today
```

Once the addresses are correctly masked, the logic works as intended.

title: probes do not run immediately
body:
### What happened?

When configuring probes for pods I expected that the probe runs immediately after waiting for the initialDelaySeconds.
but It only ran after initialDelaySeconds + periodSeconds


### What did you expect to happen?

That the probe runs immediately after waiting for initialDelaySeconds.
for example: a probe after 60 seconds and an another one at 120 seconds.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

            startupProbe:
              initialDelaySeconds: 60
              periodSeconds: 60

I think this is the expected behavior, not a bug. Kubelet starts a ticker in the probe worker with the interval set by `PeriodSeconds` and calls `doProbe()`.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.7/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L148
Inside `doProbe()`, it retrieves the pod's start time and checks whether `InitialDelaySeconds` has passed. If it hasn't, the probe is not executed.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.30.7/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go#L269

Since `PeriodSeconds` and `InitialDelaySeconds` have the same value in the manifest above, the probe simply isn't executed until the next `InitialDelaySeconds` interval has passed. Adjusting the values of `PeriodSeconds` and `InitialDelaySeconds` should bring the behavior closer to what you expect.

In our documentation we state:

> initialDelaySeconds: Number of seconds after the container has started before startup, liveness or readiness probes are initiated. If a startup probe is defined, liveness and readiness probe delays do not begin until the startup probe has succeeded. If the value of periodSeconds is greater than initialDelaySeconds then the initialDelaySeconds will be ignored. Defaults to 0 seconds. Minimum value is 0.

However, we haven't documented the case where `initialDelaySeconds` and `periodSeconds` are equal. If the first probe might be skipped due to time alignment issues, we should explicitly mention this scenario in the documentation.

@toVersus Oke Thanks for the info. It als does it when the values are different. I found another solution for my problem so its not a problem anymore.

It just seemed weird that the probe would only trigger at the end of the periodSeconds and not at the beginning.

I added debug log and found that the probe seems to be skipped because it's based on the container's `startedAt` time rather than the container's probe start time, causing it to be rounded.

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go b/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go
index 159112cfcb3..e77de30a25f 100644
--- a/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go
+++ b/pkg/kubelet/prober/worker.go
@@ -271,7 +272,10 @@ func (w *worker) doProbe(ctx context.Context) (keepGoing bool) {
        }

        // Probe disabled for InitialDelaySeconds.
-       if int32(time.Since(c.State.Running.StartedAt.Time).Seconds()) < w.spec.InitialDelaySeconds {
+       startedAt := int32(time.Since(c.State.Running.StartedAt.Time).Seconds())
+       if startedAt < w.spec.InitialDelaySeconds {
+               klog.V(3).InfoS("Initial delay not yet elapsed",
+                       "pod", klog.KObj(w.pod), "containerName", w.container.Name, "startedAt", startedAt, "initialDelay", w.spec.InitialDelaySeconds)
                return true
        }
```

Sample manifest:

```yaml
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
```

@adrianmoisey 
Today,if I set up multiple GPU servers, including H200, A100, V100, and P100, with the following IP addresses:
10.190.1.1 (H200)
10.190.1.2 (A100)
10.190.1.3 (V100)
10.190.1.4 (P100)
I have created ClearML sessions on all these servers. However, when I try to access a session via SSH, for example:
ssh 10.190.1.1 -p 30001
I am unable to log in. It seems that the issue occurs because there is also a session running on 10.190.1.2 using the same port (30001), which might be causing the system to misidentify the connection.

Additionally, we noticed that if we set up an LLM service on both 10.190.1.1:30001 and 10.190.1.2:30001, calling the service on 10.190.1.1 sometimes results in the request being handled by 10.190.1.2, which is incorrect.

We are unsure what is causing this issue. Could you please help us identify the problem and provide a solution?

Thank you!

> According to the principles of NodePort operation in Kubernetes, this issue should not occur.

what do you mean exactly? 

Are you setting you using hostNetwork pods with the ssh servers listening on the node port range?

For example, we created two pods with SSH servers (pod A and pod B) on different nodes (`10.190.1.1` and `10.190.1.2`). Both pods have the label `ai.allegro.agent.serial: pod-1`, and we applied the following service YAML file to connect to the pods via SSH.

```yaml
kind: Service
apiVersion: v1
metadata:
  name: clearml-agent-nodeport-1
  namespace: clearml
spec:
  ports:
  - name: clearml-agent-ssh
    port: 10022
    targetPort: 10022
    nodePort: 30001
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    ai.allegro.agent.serial: pod-1

```

We expect that SSH into pod A will not connect to pod B, but sometimes it connects to the wrong pod. Is there something wrong with our settings?

> We expect that SSH into pod A will not connect to pod B, but sometimes it connects to the wrong pod. Is there something wrong with our settings?

if you ssh to a NodePort of a Service it will loadbalance the traffic to the Pods that match the selector.

If you want to allow to ssh to a specific Pod, or either you define one Service NodePort per Pod , so any NodePort in any node will send the traffic to that Pod.
Or you use the Pod `HostPort` feature to publish the ssh pod in the Node where the Pod is running 
```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
    - containerPort: 10022
       hostPort: 30002
```

title: SELinux controller does not work when KCM runs in a container
body:
### What happened?

When KCM runs in a container (such as in a kops cluster), the SELinuxWarning controller does not do anything, because it thinks that SELinux is disabled - it reads /etc/selinux and /sys/fs/selinux to detect so here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/20b12ad5c389ff74792988bf1e0c10fe2820d9a1/pkg/volume/util/selinux.go#L109

As result, it does not emit useful warnings.

### What did you expect to happen?

The controller emits events, regardless if it can access /etc or /sys on the host. The controller must be explicitly enabled, so it can expect that someone who enabled it also enabled SELinux on nodes.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run KCM with `--controllers=*,selinux-warning-controller --feature-gates=SELinuxChangePolicy=true,SELinuxMount=true` and create 2 pods that use the same volume, but each Pod has different `seLinuxOptions`.

Right now (today's master) we do expect identical configuration, but that's being changed in #130037. KCM won't make any assumption about the SELinux config on any node and won't compare labels that it can't compare (can't get node's defaults)

nodes.title: selinux: add a new SELinux translator to the controller
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind feature

Fixes: #130036
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
KCM cannot read host's `/etc/selinux` to read the defaults, because it often runs as in a container with no access to host's `/etc` or `/sys`.  Therefore implement a custom `SELinuxOptionsToFileLabel` that does not default fields in SELinuxOptions and uses just fields provided by the Pod.

Since the controller cannot default empty SELinux label components, treat them as incomparable.
Example: "system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c1,c2" *does not* conflict with ":::s0:c1,c2", because the node that will run such a Pod may expand "":::s0:c1,c2" to "system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c1,c2".
However, "system_u:system_r:container_t:s0:c1,c2" *does* conflict with ":::s0:c98,c99".

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixed SELinuxWarningController defaults when running kube-controller-manager in a container.
```

#### Additional documentation e.g., KEPs (Kubernetes Enhancement Proposals), usage docs, etc.:
Enhancement issue: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/1710
```docs
- [KEP]: https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/tree/master/keps/sig-storage/1710-selinux-relabeling
```

title: CVE-2025-0426: Node Denial of Service via kubelet Checkpoint API
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where a large number of container checkpoint requests made to the unauthenticated kubelet read-only HTTP endpoint may cause a Node Denial of Service by filling the Node's disk. 

### Am I vulnerable?

All clusters running an affected version listed below with the kubelet read-only HTTP port enabled and using a container runtime that supports the container checkpointing feature, such as CRI-O v1.25.0+ (with `enable_criu_support` set to true) or containerd v2.0+ with `criu` installed, are affected.

#### Affected Versions

- kubelet v1.32.0 to v1.32.1
- kubelet v1.31.0 to v1.31.5
- kubelet v1.30.0 to v1.30.9

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by setting the `ContainerCheckpoint` feature gate to `false` in your kubelet configuration, disabling the kubelet read-only port, and limiting access to the kubelet API, or upgrading to a fixed version listed below, which enforces authentication for the kubelet Checkpoint API.

#### Fixed Versions

- kubelet master - fixed by #129739
- kubelet v1.32.2 - fixed by #130010
- kubelet v1.31.6 - fixed by #130011
- kubelet v1.30.10 - fixed by #130012
- kubelet v1.29.14 - fixed by #130014
  - Note: Container checkpoint support was an off by default Alpha feature in v1.25-v1.29

### Detection

A large number of requests to the kubelet read-only HTTP server's `/checkpoint` endpoint, or a large number of checkpoints stored (by default) under `/var/lib/kubelet/checkpoints` on a Node may indicate an attempted Denial of Service attack using this bug.

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported and fixed by Tim Allclair @tallclair from Google.

The issue was coordinated by: 

Tim Allclair @tallclair
Sascha Grunert saschagrunert@
Craig Ingram @cji
Jordan Liggitt liggitt@

/triage accepted
/lifecycle frozen

/kind bug
/committee security-response

/sig node
/area kubelet

@cji looking at the PR in question: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e62ce1c9db2dadf225f37fe3dc943b64dc251950/pkg/kubelet/server/server.go#L310-L311

It looks like we moved the section that registers the `checkpoint` url to under the `--enable-debugging-handlers` as mitigation. Am i reading this right? thanks!

https://cs.k8s.io/?q=EnableDebuggingHandlers%7CInstallDebuggingHandlers&i=nope&literal=nope&files=&excludeFiles=api%7Cstaging%7Ctest%7Ckubemark&repos=kubernetes/kubernetes

> It looks like we moved the section that registers the checkpoint url to under the --enable-debugging-handlers as mitigation. Am i reading this right? thanks!

Yes, correct. Except "Debugging Handlers" is misrepresentative here. Default handlers get installed on both the unauthenticated "read only" port, and the authenticated port, while "debugging handlers" are only ever installed on the authenticated port. I have a first pass at making this obvious in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129354, but we should probably also consider improving the documentation to the `EnableDebuggingHandlers` option.

@tallclair thank you for the explanation!

Hi everyone,

For those of you who may experience a lengthy Kubelet update process, will setting the read-only port to 0 be able to protect us?

> This means If the checkpoint for runc, crun or youki fails, does this mean that this CVE is not affected?

This CVE applies to clusters using any underlying CRI implementation that supports checkpointing. containerd and CRI-O were provided as non-exhaustive examples of "a container runtime that supports the container checkpointing feature".

> For those of you who may experience a lengthy Kubelet update process, will setting the read-only port to 0 be able to protect us?

Disabling the read-only port mitigates this issue by only allowing the checkpoint API to be accessed behind authentication.

title: Kubelet serving CSR never created
body:
### What happened?

We are seeing an issue occasionally where the kubelet never gets the server certificate (`serverTLSBootstrap: true`).
We have an auto-approver for the server certificates and detect this issue because we are waiting for the certificate to appear in `/var/lib/kubelet/pki/kubelet-server-current.pem`. When we hit it, not even the CSR is created.
It started happening after upgrading to v1.32 so we believe it could be from a change that was introduced in v1.32.
Restarting the kubelet does not help. It happily continues without the server certificate, even though it is configured to bootstrap it.

In healthy clusters, we see this:

```console
$ kubectl get csr
NAME        AGE   SIGNERNAME                                    REQUESTOR                           REQUESTEDDURATION   CONDITION
csr-8dql4   29s   kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving                 system:node:lennart-kubelet-debug   <none>              Pending
csr-r8ztr   17s   kubernetes.io/kubelet-serving                 system:node:lennart-kubelet-debug   <none>              Pending
csr-xtwpf   30s   kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet   system:node:lennart-kubelet-debug   <none>              Approved,Issued
```

In faulty clusters, there is just the client CSR.
~~We are not sure why two CSRs are created for the server either, but it works when we approve the newer of them.~~

Edit: The two server CSRs happen because kubeadm restarts the kubelet as part of initializing. This is how it picks up the client certificate. After the restart, the kubelet does not "remember" its old server CSR so it creates a new. This is not an issue.

Here is the kubelet config from an affected node: [kubelet-config.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/18688742/kubelet-config.txt)

### What did you expect to happen?

When configured, the kubelet should always create the server CSR.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Unfortunately we do not have any guaranteed reproduction steps.
In general, this is what is needed to trigger the issue:

1. Kubelet is configured to rotate certificates (default) and to use server certificate.
2. Node status is stable, i.e. there are no changes of any kind that would cause the kubelet to update the status.
3. Kubelet is restarted and the server certificate does not exist (e.g. because it was removed or it wasn't issued yet).

In this specific case you should be able to see that the CSR is not created:

```console
$ kubectl get csr
NAME        AGE   SIGNERNAME                                    REQUESTOR                           REQUESTEDDURATION   CONDITION
csr-2mq8h   22s   kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client-kubelet   system:node:lennart-kubelet-debug   <none>              Approved,Issued
$ kubectl get nodes
NAME                    STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
lennart-kubelet-debug   Ready    control-plane   28s   v1.32.1
```

### Anything else we need to know?

I believe the culprit is https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640. Not the randomization of the interval, but the change in how the [zero case for the lastStatusReportTime](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640/files#diff-f39bb531745e5658a65143c9054c3fa92aa3ac9f41e9e627ac61b7ff08808153R607) is handled.
It used to be treated as expired and trigger an update. After the PR it is treated the opposite.
This means that `patchNodeStatus` is never called and consequently neither is `setLastObservedNodeAddresses`.
The latter is initializing the kubelets internal node address state (not node status).
This internal state is what the server certificate manager is relying on to create the CSR. As long as it is `nil`, i.e. as long as the node status hasn't been patched, it cannot progress.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
Client Version: v1.32.1
Kustomize Version: v5.5.0
Server Version: v1.32.1
```

</details>


### Cloud provider

<details>
Happens both with and without external cloud provider
</details>


### OS version

<details>

```console
# On Linux:
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here
```

</details>

In this run I started with kubelet stopped and did the following:
1. kubeadm init and wait
2. approve the (second) kubelet serving CSR
3. kubeadm reset

The final `Stopping kubelet.service` comes from kubeadm reset.
So is a kubeadm process thing?

Yes, I found the code in kubeadm now that does this: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2b3da7dfc846fec7c4044a320f8f38b4a45367a3/cmd/kubeadm/app/cmd/phases/init/kubeletfinalize.go#L146
I wonder if there could be some very particular order of events that could cause issues here. As far as I understand we have at least three things happening in parallel here:

1. kubeadm going through the init process, which ends with a kubelet restart during [kubelet-finalize] before the [addons] phase
2. kubelet client certificate rotation happening in the background
3. kubelet server certificate rotation happening in the background

The happy/normal case seems to be that the CSRs are created, kubelet registers the node and kubeadm restarts the kubelet. Then another CSR is created for the server certificate, because the first one was "forgotten" and most likely didn't get approved in time for the restart.
What I don't know is what would happen if the order is different, and is it even possible for them to be different? Perhaps kubeadm is waiting on something that always happens after the client CSR? Is it possible that kubeadm restarts the kubelet during a sensitive step that could somehow make it permanently stuck?
tagging kubeadm maintainers that are better positioned to answer these questions @neolit123 @fabriziopandini

> When we hit it, not even the CSR is created.
> It started happening after upgrading to v1.32 so we believe it could be from a change that was introduced in v1.32.

kubeadm has no recent changes related to the kubelet-finalize phase (minus [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/6e17cc7f0eaa4718951129e75d615abedebba65e)). that phase requires the kubelet restart to truly enable kubelet client cert rotation.

> What I don't know is what would happen if the order is different, and is it even possible for them to be different? Perhaps kubeadm is waiting on something that always happens after the client CSR? Is it possible that kubeadm restarts the kubelet during a sensitive step that could somehow make it permanently stuck?

kubeadm does the following on join:
- writes a bootstrap-kubelet.conf
- starts the kubelet with client cert rotation enabled (default from config)
- waits for the kubelet to write a kubelet.conf file (that means csr was sent and tls bootstrap completed)

on init:
- writes directly a kubelet.conf
- starts the kubelet with client cert rotation enabled by default (from config)
- waits for the control plane to start up
- mutates the kubelet.conf to point to the client certs on disk and restarts the kubelet (kubelet-finalize phase)

if the kubelet knows about the requirement for server cert rotation (from config) but it never creates the csr due to restarts, that seems like a kubelet bug.

I think I figured it out! In https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640, the [isUpdateStatusPeriodExperid](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L605-L608C3) was introduced with these lines:

```go
	if kl.lastStatusReportTime.IsZero() {
		return false
	}
```

Doesn't that mean that the period is not expired ever, until we have the first status report? That makes [tryUpdateNodeStatus](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L559) return early:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L584-L586

Why is that a problem if the Node status didn't change? Well, it means that we never call patchNodeStatus, so we never initialize the last observed node address:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L663-L670

This means that we can never create the CSR, because we do not know what addresses to use!

Usually this is not an issue, because there are many changes to the node when starting up the first time. However, when the kubelet is restarted later, e.g. as part of cert-rotation, there are no changes that makes it update the status.

To summarize, I think we should change `isUpdateStatusPeriodExperid` to return `true` always if `kl.lastStatusReportTime.IsZero()` to make sure that things are initialized.

> To summarize, I think we should change `isUpdateStatusPeriodExperid` to return `true` always if `kl.lastStatusReportTime.IsZero()` to make sure that things are initialized.

@lentzi90 before we didn't update the node if it didn't change

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blame/3184eb3d1b2b07b3b68eff5240eb8a8e20bb0d07/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L484-L488

```
	node, changed := kl.updateNode(ctx, originalNode)

	if !changed {
		// We don't do markVolumesFromNode(node) here and leave it to the regular syncNodeStatus().
		return false
	}
```

so that logic looks correct, if there was no update and the node didn't change, we don't update.

I think we need to understand what is the heuristic to detect the node change

EDIT

ups, wrong, place , there are two loops that update the node `fastNodeStatusUpdate` and `tryUpdateNodeStatus`, you are changing the later, taking a look now 👀

Adding for reference how the server CSR is created:
1. [NewServerCertificateManager called from NewMainKubelet](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go#L841) with [getLastObservedNodeAddresses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L752) as `getAddresses` func
2. [getTemplate](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/931ad2a9fdedaf1e47126f5b3e5880eb3708bfb2/pkg/kubelet/certificate/kubelet.go#L123) function constructed from `getAddresses` and [returns nil](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/931ad2a9fdedaf1e47126f5b3e5880eb3708bfb2/pkg/kubelet/certificate/kubelet.go#L60) when no addresses can be found.
3. The certificate manager [returns early](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/util/certificate/certificate_manager.go#L429-L430) if `getTemplate` returns `nil` and the CSR is never created.

All of this is based on the `getLastObservedNodeAddresses` returning `nil`, which it does until [setLastObservedNodeAddresses](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L747-L750) has been called. It is only called from [patchNodeStatus](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L670), which in turn only happens when the node changed or is considered expired:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L584-L598. 
I can see it is also called from [fastNodeStatusUpdate here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ad4d9b2f5119f2bcf742239018a397d3794cb6e0/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L503). Need to look through that code also.

Ok looks like the `fastNodeStatusUpdate` was always returning early if no change needed to be reported. I think that means we were relying on the `tryUpdateNodeStatus` previous behavior where it determined it like this:

```go
shouldPatchNodeStatus := changed || kl.clock.Since(kl.lastStatusReportTime) >= kl.nodeStatusReportFrequency
```

> were relying on the `tryUpdateNodeStatus` previous behavior where it determined it like this:

I see, and `kl.clock.Since(kl.lastStatusReportTime)` was `now - zero` , that is why it got triggered

@lentzi90 either way it seems odd that we rely on a blind update for this, I get a bit lost on the latest development, can you please clarify what is the node state that change and why we don't detect it, but once it updates the objects it is fixed?

That's the thing, there is no change.
We remove the old certificates, add a bootstrap config and restart the kubelet to force a certificate rotation. The Node did not change in any way, but due to the restart, `lastObservedNodeAddresses` will be `nil` until `setLastObservedNodeAddresses` is called. It seems that it is only ever called when we patch the node, and there is no reason to patch since there is no change.

There are probably other ways to make sure `lastObservedNodeAddresses` is set though. And strictly speaking we do not need to patch the Node, we just need to set the kubelet state.

One thing is still unclear to me. The client CSR somehow still gets created. I will try to figure out how that code path looks like. Maybe it is not relying on the same?

Ok the client CSR was simple. In that case we only [need the node name](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0b1ef24a9912d1cbbbfe5641bf9cd2cdc91f32bd/pkg/kubelet/certificate/kubelet.go#L231-L235) so there is no reason to get any addresses.

**Summarizing my understanding**

Before https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640:
- `patchNodeStatus` was always called after `nodeStatusReportFrequency` even if there was no change

After https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640:
- `patchNodeStatus` will ONLY be called if `lastStatusReportTime` is != 0 and the period expired (or the node changed).
`lastStatusReportTime` is 0 initially, so as long as there is no update to the node it will never update its status.
That in itself is probably not an issue if the node didn't change. But it also means that `getLastObservedNodeAddresses` will return `nil` during all this time. That also means that during all this time the server CSR cannot be created.

What seems odd to me is that the zero time is handled separately. It was not before so why now? Shouldn't the kubelet update the status always with `nodeStatusReportFrequency`? After https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640, it does not do that until there is an actual change to it. Only after that does it respect the `nodeStatusReportFrequency`.

> After [#128640](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/128640), it does not do that until there is an actual change to it. Only after that does it respect the `nodeStatusReportFrequency`.

yep, I think you are right, that looks wrong, it should start reporting periodically

nodes.title: Use node addresses from informer in kubelet certificate manager
nodes.body:
The kubelet certificate manager was using a closure to get the node addresses, but this closure depended on a static field that was only updated during the node status update. This created a twisted dependency between the node.status reconcile loops and the certificate manager.

This commit fixes this issue by using the node informer to get the node addresses directly. This ensures that the kubelet always requests a certificate with the latest node addresses.

/kind bug
/kind cleanup

Fixes #130001

```release-note
NONE
```

/sig node
/sig network

Thanks for catching this!

So this issue was happening particularly for the `componentGlobalsRegistry` flags because of 2 things:

1. We populate the [Options.Flagz](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/options/options.go#L51) [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/pkg/controlplane/apiserver/options/options.go#L262) which is populated using [ServerRunOptions.Flags()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/options/completion.go#L60)

2. The [ServerRunOptions.Flags()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/options/completion.go#L60) calls [ComponentGlobalsRegistry.AddFlags()](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/options/server_run_options.go#L378) which would reset emulationVersion and featureGates flags [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/39f1c90ac014828803a156b40d49f0c58fb7384a/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/compatibility/registry.go#L229-L231) everytime this function was invoked ultimately causing those to show empty in /flagz endpoint

Two potential solutions to this problem are:

1. Store the parsed flag values directly in Options.Flagz [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L134) upon initial parsing. This would eliminate the need to call ServerRunOptions.Flags() [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/options/completion.go#L60) again to retrieve the same information.

2. As a complementary measure, wrap the ServerRunOptions.Flags() function with sync.Once() to ensure it is executed only once.

When `func (s *ServerRunOptions) Flags()` is called, a new set of flags are created. The `cmd.Flags()` are parsed and set before the `Complete()`. I am not sure if you would be able to capture the flags set from `fs := cmd.Flags()` in the flagz

I think both cmd.Flags() and ServerRunOptions.Flags() end up pointing to the same underlying Flag objects when we merge the two [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/release-1.32/cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go#L130-L132) so flagz should have contents from both, but cmd.Flags() overrides the ServerRunOptions.Flags().

@sttts since you initially helped review the [apiserver-flagz endpoint PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127581), could you please help verify if the above understanding is correct?

> When `func (s *ServerRunOptions) Flags()` is called, a new set of flags are created. The `cmd.Flags()` are parsed and set before the `Complete()`. I am not sure if you would be able to capture the flags set from `fs := cmd.Flags()` in the flagz

It would capture though it is a new flagSet, because it still points to the same pointer variables(`(s *ServerRunOptions)`) as the flags' value.

However, in the proposed fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/129996, it passes in the same flagSets in case there is any reset happen between flag parsing and flagz reading.

title: Excessive conntrack cleanup causes high memory (12GB) and CPU usage when any Pod with a UDP port changes
body:
### What happened? We are encountering a severe performance issue in kube-proxy (v1.32) when any Pod with a UDP port is updated (e.g., CoreDNS). In the new kube-proxy implementation, changes to Services or Pods that expose UDP ports trigger a full conntrack cleanup. This cleanup process iterates over the entire conntrack table, leading to extremely high resource consumption—sometimes up to 12 GB of memory and 1.5 CPU cores per kube-proxy instance. In a simple test, we observed 2,780 instances of the log message "Adding conntrack filter for cleanup", which caused an OOM when kube-proxy was limited to 256 MB of memory. Without that limit, kube-proxy memory usage spiked to 12 GB. On nodes with large conntrack tables, kube-proxy effectively becomes stuck, consuming all available memory each time there is a UDP endpoint change. This issue appears to be systemic; every change in a Pod with a UDP port triggers all kube-proxy instances to perform the extensive cleanup. Currently, there is no option to disable or throttle this behavior, which disrupts cluster stability and can lead to service degradation or outages. We request that the cleanup logic be revised to target only the relevant conntrack entries or that a mechanism be provided to disable or limit this aggressive cleanup behavior. https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/127318 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130 ### What did you expect to happen? We expected kube-proxy to handle conntrack cleanup in a more efficient and targeted way. Even if it needs to scan a significant portion of the conntrack table, it should do so without causing a spike to 12 GB of memory usage. Ideally, it would either: - Limit its cleanup to entries relevant to the specific changed UDP endpoint. - Provide a way to configure or disable this aggressive cleanup process so it does not risk out-of-memory (OOM) events or excessively high CPU usage. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - Deploy multiple Pods that generate a high volume of DNS requests, for example: - A simple Golang application making repeated DNS lookups without any caching mechanism. - Observe kube-proxy resource usage (memory and CPU) on that node. - Delete or update the coredns Pod (which also uses UDP DNS). - Watch the logs and resource usage of kube-proxy closely, noting the surge in memory (potentially up to 12 GB) and CPU usage as it performs the conntrack cleanup. ### Anything else we need to know? ![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f75f0bc0-e394-45fa-b323-2f6fc0570386) ### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.31.2 Kustomize Version: v5.4.2 Server Version: v1.32.0-eks-5ca49cb ```
### Cloud provider
AWS
### OS version
```console # On Linux: Amazon Linux 2 5.10.230-223.885.amzn2.aarch64 ```
### Install tools
EKS
### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)
containerd://1.7.23
### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)
kube-proxy:v1.32.0-minimal-eksbuild.2

service-ip here can be one of ClusterIP, LoadBalancerIP or ExternalIP. I think it is safe to assume that all flow entries with destination as a ClusterIP will be owned by kube-proxy, but not for LoadBalancerIPs and ExternalIPs.

I can think of three ways to figure out if a conntrack flow is owned by kube-proxy:
1. Using service port and target port for filtering
   --orig-dst=`<service_ip>` && --orig-port-dst=`<service_port>` && --reply-port-src=`<endpoint/target_port>`
   This is not a full-proof solution but should cover almost all the cases.
2. Using pod-cidr
    We can filter out kube-proxy owned flows first  using --orig-dst=`<service_ip>` and --reply-src=`<belongs to pod-cidr>`. 
    Though this can mis the cases of pods running in host network namespace.
3. Using conntrack labels (as Dan suggested [here](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/126130#issuecomment-2348883750) )
 
[1] seems a straight forward way [2] and [3] may required API changes.

1. Revert conntrack reconciler #130479 
2. fix forward https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484 , traffic to a ClusterIP|ExternalIP|LoadBalancerIP:Port is forwarded by kube-proxy rules, so it can only be directed to a Service,=. NodePorts are special as can be directed to any IP on the node, but NodePort ranges are reserved, so *:NodePort can only match Services. I don't see what other thing can match there, that was my original idea and I missed it during the review, sorry about that

I was trying to understand the blast radius and I didn't find a large impact, @sergeylanzman did you solve the problem with the first patch, @brandond do you have more reports than the one linked here?

Ok, it seems the problem is more contained than I thought, is a second bug that exacerbated the first one, more entries more memory, and that only should impact kube-proxy CPU consumption and consequent host performance impact. Increasing the `--iptables-min-sync-period duration` will alleviate the problem, since the reconciler will run every that period.

The problem is that we were not checking the Service Ports on the conntrack entries, hence any UDP traffic associated to a Service IP was deleted, and since overlays CNIs like flannel use to use UDP for traffic (vxlan), any new inter node traffic will create new entries that will be deleted again, it was easy to reproduce even with an unit test  https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484#discussion_r1976011944 . This also explains this comment https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129982#issuecomment-2639495058,   that was puzzling me, how is possible we were matching so many stale entries on the conntrack reconciler filters.

This is the PR with the fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484#issuecomment-2691561466 , 
I think that for 1.33 we are fine and we don't need to revert, the bug is clear and a quick analysis on my side didn't find much evidence this has a large impact, any ClusterIP service will not likely be impacted, LoadBalancerIPs use to be independent IPs that are filtered to receive traffic only on the ServicePorts ... that leaves us to ExternalIPs that are not very recommended https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97110 these days , not saying is not an ugly bug, but I want to put into context, since I also think we may decide to backport the fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484 instead of reverting the reconciler in 1.32 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130481

K3s (and RKE2 under some configurations) make extensive use of LoadBalancer services where the LB IP is the Node IP or ExternalIP. Anything that continues to cause problems in this configuration wouldn't be great for us.

> K3s (and RKE2 under some configurations) make extensive use of LoadBalancer services where the LB IP is the Node IP or ExternalIP. Anything that continues to cause problems in this configuration wouldn't be great for us.

Nothing can keep causing problems in any configuration, we need to fix all the problems, the question is what solution do we use for it.
I'm happy that I could easily reproduce the bug so I'm confident on the fix https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130484, we will not need revert the reconciler in 1.33.

For 1.32 we can backport the fix or revert the reconciler (the reconciler fixed 2 long standing bugs related to udp), at the beginning I was not even thinking in a backport, after this was a second bug, but now after checking the fix and that the first bug was in the library not in the logic, and there is no functional regression, I think is a possibility the backport https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/130505
I also had this issue using `v1.32.0-eksbuild.2` and the workaround was to patch the the kube-proxy daemonset with `v1.31.10-minimal-eksbuild.2`

The backport of the fix landed in 1.32.3 https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b0554e32c769fe68eb2bd770134bbb03b9a41eea .
Also, the latest patch release for 1.32 branch is in 1.32.8, you should try to be on the latest patch release of each branch to get the fixes

For anyone landing here later: this issue is closed/fixed, and the backport landed in v1.32.3 (see commit: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b0554e32c769fe68eb2bd770134bbb03b9a41eea). If you still see the same behavior on provider builds (e.g. EKS kube-proxy addons lagging behind), double-check you’re running a kube-proxy build that includes that backport (or move to the latest v1.32 patch for your branch).

  If you’re stuck waiting for the provider addon update, one mitigation mentioned in this thread was increasing `--iptables-min-sync-period` to reduce how often the sync path runs. It
  doesn’t fix the root cause, but it can reduce the blast radius.

  Quick sanity checks:
  ```bash
  kubectl -n kube-system top pods -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
  # on an affected node:
  cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_{count,max}
```

nodes.title: conntrack reconciler must check the dst port
nodes.body:
/kind bug
/kind regression

Fixes #129982

Services can expose applications on a tuple IP:Port, where IP can be ClusterIP|ExternalP|LoadBalancerIP:ServicePort or *:NodePort. We also have the list of IPs with the backends associated.

When implementing a reconcilation loop for conntrack we have a list of this tuples, we match the conntrack entries that match the frontend tuple IP:Port or *:NodePort and we removes the entries that does not have a known endpoints.

However, during the implementation we forget to check for the ServicePort, causing that the reconciler got busy with any IP on a Service that had a large amount of UDP entries , specially problematic on Services with ExternalIPs and use overlay, since those use UDP for encapsulation extensevely.


```release-note
Fixes a 1.32 regression kube-proxy, when using a Service with External or LoadBalancer IPs on UDP services , was consuming a large amount of CPU because it was not filtering by the Service destination port and trying to delete all the UDP entries associated to the service.
```

I think this might be due to the `.spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` option on the Deployment itself, which defaults to 600 seconds and fails the deployment if the deadline is exceeded ([docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/#progress-deadline-seconds)), rather than the timeout on the deployment watch in the kubectl cli

It is right that `spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` can cause a deployment to fail before `kubectl rollout status --timeout=20m` completes, but it's separate from the CLI timeout. The former is enforced at the cluster level, while --timeout only controls how long kubectl waits.

nodes.title: Fix service account node audience restriction for in-tree pv to csi migration
nodes.body:
Translate in-tree inline volume or in-tree persistent volumes to CSI using the CSI translator while verifying whether the kubelet is allowed to request a token for an audience when enforcing service account node audience restrictions.

fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129935

```release-note
Fixes a regression with the ServiceAccountNodeAudienceRestriction feature where `azureFile` volumes encounter "failed to get service accoount token attributes" errors
```

title: Pods with postStart lifecycle hook are stuck in Pending state.
body:
### What happened?

Upon kubernetes control plane v1.32 upgrade pods with **postStart** lifecycle hook configured are unable to start.
Pod is failing to report its state and remains in **Pending** state forever.
Also it's impossible to path or update deployment like change replicas number or image tag, not possible to delete pod without --force flag.
But it allows to update deployment to remove **lifecycle** section.

### What did you expect to happen?

Pod should start normally, lifecycle hook must be processed.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Tested on v1.32.0 (v1.32.0-gke.1448000, v1.32.0-eks-5ca49cb) and v1.32.1 (v1.32.1-gke.1002000)

Create deployment on cluster v1.32, postStart lifecycle hook must be defined as below:
```
lifecycle:
  postStart:
    sleep:
      seconds: 15
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Some details.

1. No issues with PreStop hooks.

2. Deployment definition used to reproduce the issue:

```
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: inflate
  labels:
    app: inflate
automountServiceAccountToken: false


---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: inflate
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: inflate
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: inflate
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: inflate
      containers:
      - args:
          - infinity
        command:
          - sleep
        image: python:3
        name: inflate
        lifecycle:
          postStart:
            sleep:
              seconds: 15
```

title: Reduce relist operations in client-go
body:
### What would you like to be added?

Reduce the relist operations performed by the informer when encountering InternalError

### Why is this needed?

Currently, parameter `MaxInternalErrorRetryDuration` exists in the reflector and is only used in the kube-apiserver. It was introduced in this [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111387) to address the issue where the kube-apiserver retrieves data from etcd via a list operation instead of resuming a watch when etcd has no leader for a period of time. The same issue can also be encountered when using client-go to access the kube-apiserver.

I encountered a live issue, and the logs show the following messages:
```shell
pkg/mod/k8s.io/client-go@v0.32.0/tools/cache/reflector.go:251: watch of *v1.Pod ended with: an error on the server ("unable to decode an event from the watch stream: got short buffer with n=0, base=4092, cap=163840") has prevented the request from succeeding
```
Currently, when the reflector encounters this error, it triggers a relist operation, which is quite costly. From the conversation https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/111387#discussion_r1304095981, this error can be resolved by resuming the watch instead of performing a relist. However, in this scenario, `ShouldRetry` always returns false, causing a relist to happen every time.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ab54e442c6cfc64d25462906c276950796e6803c/staging/src/k8s.io/client-go/tools/cache/reflector.go#L530-L534

At the same time, I have a question: InternalError is quite vague. Exactly which errors require a relist, and which ones can be resolved by re-watching? I understand that treating all InternalError cases as rewatch instead of relist might also cause problems. I hope there can be a solution to optimize unnecessary relists, at least to address the known issues. Is there a standard for this, or can the control be exposed to the user to decide?

/sig api-machinery
@wojtek-t @liggitt how do you guys thing about this

If an InternalError occurs, relist seems to be intuitive. It is an internal error and the entire process needs to be retried. In addition, the frequency of occurrence does not seem to be reflected in the issue? If the frequency is very high, do we need to refine the error code? Also, is there any way to reproduce ?

I think i have found the reason. Refer to [Fix client watch reestablishment handling of client-side timeouts](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/89652) which is used to fix reflector behavior when it encounters watch decode errors because of client-side timeouts.

There is an issue in the `Read` logic of the current implementation of `lengthDelimitedFrameReader`

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0798325ba13643358aa3ebb7c6ddc3006ac26a7c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/util/framer/framer.go#L92-L96

When executing the `io.ReadAtLeast` on line 92, if a client timeout happens at that exact moment, n will be 0, and err will be a timeout error, such as context deadline exceeded. However, **on line 95, the original err is masked and replaced with `io.ErrShortBuffer`.** 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/0798325ba13643358aa3ebb7c6ddc3006ac26a7c/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/runtime/serializer/streaming/streaming.go#L76-L81

`d.reader` is the `lengthDelimitedFrameReader` mentioned above. If the issue described earlier occurs, the result at line 77 will be 0 and `io.ErrShortBuffer`. Then, when execution reaches line 80, a completely custom error will be returned.


https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/2334b8469e1983c525c0c6382125710093a25883/staging/src/k8s.io/apimachinery/pkg/watch/streamwatcher.go#L113-L122

Due to the issue mentioned above, net.IsTimeout(err) will be false. It will then send an event to `sw.result` with the type StatusInternalServerError.

The relist operation was triggered unexpectedly in the reflector finally.

/assign @liggitt 
/assign @wojtek-t 

thx~
Thanks for the detailed report / root-cause, I'll defer this to api-machinery triage to prioritize / route

title: Long Lived TCP Connections Fail When Downscaling Kube Proxy (ExternalTrafficPolicy Cluster)
body:
### What happened?

Some external cloud providers such as Azure use a pass-through(direct server return) load balancer. This means that TCP connections are not terminated on the loadbalancer, but instead downstream in the kubernetes cluster.

ExternalTrafficPolicy Cluster configures load balancers to send traffic to any node in the cluster, even if the node is not running a pod that the traffic is destined to. From there kube-proxy routes the request to the pod (which could either be on the same or different node). 

In our case, when client sets up a long living TCP connection and that traffic path hits kube-proxy on a node that downscales sometime during the duration of the TCP connection, we observe 520 errors from the server. 

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubernetes nodes that act as a intermediate hop between the loadbalancer and the node/pod that the traffic is destined to should gracefully allow all existing TCP connections to finish before the node/processes are terminated. 

This is important because some loadbalancers like Azure continue to send traffic to existing TCP even though the target node has been marked unheathly.  

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1) Setup any service (e.g., nginx ingress), tolerated/tainted to node group A. Use loadbalancer with external traffic policy: cluster. 
2) Scale node pool B. 
3) Simulate many http requests, targetting loadbalancer endpoint of service created in step 1
4) Scale down node pool B.
5) Observe errors on requests that proxied through scaled down node in node pool B. 

### Anything else we need to know?

I do suspect there might be a need for cloud-specific solutions to this, as each cloud's LB has its own idiosyncracies. For instance, Azure LBs are pass-through and also, upon a node being marked unhealthy, all existing TCP connections to said node will continue to be passed through to it. This is a super fun issue.  What you want is a way to know a) this node is going to go away "soon"; and b) to possible delay that act.  We do not have a formal node termination lifecycle - there are several implementations, but they mostly follow the pattern of:
- cordon the node (make it unschedulable)
- drain the node (via an external control loop)
- turn off the VM
- delete the Node resource

Initially I hoped that we could use cordon as a signal to indicate this node is going away, but it turns out that some people use it for other reasons, and we cannot over-assume what it means.

So we modified kube-proxy's healthz in response to the "ToBeDeletedByClusterAutoscaler" taint (which was called out in 
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/129605#issuecomment-2593579402).

This at least allows upstream LBs to HC-fail nodes that are going out of service, and stop routing new traffic through them.  It requires the LB implementations to adopt this pattern*, and it doesn't really address long-lived connections.

Unfortunately, we don't have great visibility into how many connections are being routed through this machine, and nobody has spent real effort to make that better.  Kube-proxy doesn't really handle the data, it just programs the kernel.  If there were a clean way to keep track of this info, perhaps we could expose it in a way that the down-scaler could be smart about.

So, I am afraid this is "working as intended" and if someone wants to try to do better (which would be great) it would require a new KEP.

* Sending LB HCs to the NodePort is suspect.  Pre-container LB's understand VMs and they need the HC to indicate whether a VM is suitable to receive traffic for a service.  All it tells you is that at least one pod is reachable from this node, but ignores whether this node is a good choice for routing or not.
thanks for the clarification @thockin , definitely helps our understanding.

So, is someone interested in trying to do better?  I'm not honestly sure what that means, concretely, but I would welcome someone to do some research and analysis of the implementations and see what's possible.

Otherwise, I think we should close this one for now?

i'd be fine with closing this, but it would be nice to hear from @philipianni to learn if they had any suggestions.

title: DRA: Using All allocation mode will schedule to nodes with zero devices
body:
### What happened?

I created a resource claim template to get "All" GPUs on a node:

```yaml
apiVersion: resource.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: ResourceClaimTemplate
metadata:
  name: all-gpus
spec:
  spec:
    devices:
      requests:
      - name: gpu
        deviceClassName: gpu.nvidia.com
        allocationMode: All
```

I then created a deployment that had a Pod that used that claim. The Pod was scheduled to a node. However, my DRA driver on that node was not running, so there were no resource slices for that node.

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the pod to not schedule, since there were no available devices meeting the request. "All" should mean "at least one".

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create the resource claim template as shown and a deployment, with no DRA driver running. The pod will still schedule.

In the mathematical sense, "all devices in an empty set" is the empty set. But I agree that the "all devices that match and at least one" is the better semantic of this feature. Let's treat it as a bug, then we can backport.

If someone really wants "all devices that match, none is okay, too" then in 1.33 they can use `firstAvailableOf` (first alternative is "all devices", second is "none").

/triage accepted
/priority important-soon
I like the idea of explicitly documenting an all-or-nothing mode. Eventually we'll find someone who'd like it, I'm sure.
/assign

The relevant code is here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/e319c541f144e9bee6160f1dd8671638a9029f4c/staging/src/k8s.io/dynamic-resource-allocation/structured/allocator.go#L200-L228

`requestData.allDevices` is currently empty and `requestData.numDevices` is 0 when a node has no devices published. One additional if check at the end might be enough. Tests will be more work... as usual.

nodes.title: DRA: fix allocation mode `All`
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?

/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

It fixes DRA allocation mode `All` in case when there are no devices available for allocation.
In the current code `All` means `All possible devices` and `no devices` matches this criteria.

Changed the code so that `All` means `at least one device`. 
Added unit tests for this use case.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

Fixes #129310

#### Special notes for your reviewer:

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?

```release-note
DRA: when asking for "All" devices on a node, Kubernetes <= 1.32 proceeded to schedule pods onto nodes with no devices by not allocating any devices for those pods. Kubernetes 1.33 changes that to only picking nodes which have at least one device. Users who want the "proceed with scheduling also without devices" semantic can use the upcoming prioritized list feature with one sub-request for "all" devices and a second alternative with "count: 0".
```

/cc @pohly @johnbelamaric

title: MutatingAdmissionPolicy mutation ordering issue
body:
### What happened?

This works:
```
    - patchType: "JSONPatch"
      jsonPatch:
        expression: >
          [
            JSONPatch{
              op: "add", path: "/spec/initContainers",
              value: []
            },
            JSONPatch{
              op: "add", path: "/spec/initContainers/-",
              value: Object.spec.initContainers{
                name: "mesh-proxy",
                image: "mesh-proxy/v1.0.0",
                restartPolicy: "Always"
              }
            }
          ]
```

But, this fails for a pod:
```
    - patchType: "JSONPatch"
      jsonPatch:
        expression: >
          [
            JSONPatch{
              op: "add", path: "/spec/initContainers",
              value: []
            }
          ]
    - patchType: "JSONPatch"
      jsonPatch:
        expression: >
          [
            JSONPatch{
              op: "add", path: "/spec/initContainers/-",
              value: Object.spec.initContainers{
                name: "mesh-proxy",
                image: "mesh-proxy/v1.0.0",
                restartPolicy: "Always"
              }
            }
          ]
```
with:
```
denied request: JSON Patch: add operation does not apply: doc is missing path: "/spec/initContainers/-": missing value
```

Seems like the ordering is wrong or the input of one isn't fed into the next

### What did you expect to happen?

Both should work

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Try chaining the mutations together in the same object, one relying on the next as above

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

nodes.body: /sig api-machinery
@knrc Thanks for reporting this.  Are you interested in proposing a PR to fix or would you prefer someone else resolve this one?

Looking at this more closely, it's less clear to me that this is the wrong behavior.

The reason the first case works is that we apply the mutations in series without interleaving in any other operations.  This allows the `value: []` to be preserved between operations.

The reason the second case fails is that we reserialize the object (and apply defaulting, I believe) and so the `value: []` is omitted, causing the second patch operation to fail. This behavior is consistent with how completely independent mutations interact in the mutation chain, so of the two behaviors, it's the more consistent one.

What I'm suggesting at is that we might not want to try to guarantee that a single JSON Patch mutations with multiple operations is the same as multiple JSON Patch mutations that perform the same operations, but as different mutations.

I can see how this can be confusing, but the only viable alternative, I think, is to change the behavior so that BOTH examples fail in the same way, and I think that results in JSON Patch being harder to use because intermediate states get wiped.

@jpbetz I'm not the reporter, that's @kfox1111, but I did take a quick look at the issue last week.  I suggested he keep this open so that it could be discussed, at the very least to document this is how it behaves.  It's the serialization between the mutations that's causing the issue, and this is likely unexpected.
@knrc gotcha. Yes, this might be best handled via documentation.

Yeah. If its working through all the patches in a row, actually allowing changes to flow from one to the next, just that the omit functionality happens to be undoing things in this example, I think that is probably okish, and there is no bug here.
/triage accepted

/close

title: There is a conflict between the metrics of controller-runtime and component-base, the metric workqueue_depth  of controller-runtime repository not  take effect
body:
### What happened?

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/blob/7399a3a595bf254add9d0c96c49af462e1aac193/pkg/metrics/workqueue.go#L99

https://github.com/kubernetes/component-base/blob/03d57670a9cda43def5d9c960823d6d4558e99ff/metrics/prometheus/workqueue/metrics.go#L101

Both repository try to set the Provider but only the earliest will take effect. In the case where component-base library is initialized first, the workqueue_depth metrics in component-base will be used and the metrics in controller-runtime will not work. It will cause the default exposed metrics in controller-runtime to be unable to show the workflow_depth number.

Is there any hint or recommendation for handling that?

### What did you expect to happen?

The  workqueue_depth  should take effect that provided by controller-runtime repository

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The component-base library might not be directly depended. However, other libraries like k8s.io/apiextensions-apiserver;if the codes in these libraries call component-base functions, the initialization function in component-base will work and might call workqueue.SetProvider before controller-runtime, which will prevent the later controller-runtime from setting its own workqueue_depth metrics.

We have several automated scripts that run kubectl commands to exec into the pods and execute some custom scripts scripts. body:
### What happened?

Recently the CMOS battery is faulty, we did a change and rebooted the node. After rebooting, we found almost of pods cannot be created by kubelet + containerd.

The timeline is like this
1. **_time:  Sep  26  19:55:45 -07 2024_**. We have a pod created at **_2024-09-05T14:20:50.537022918-07:00_**
  ```
 aff8aea34f502       4 weeks ago         Ready            x-generic22-kdw2k              sdprod              0                   (default)
  ```
2. Shutdown and change the CMOS battery, the time is set to **_Tue Nov 21 13:57 - 05:46_**. 
3. After rebooting the node, kubelet started to work before time is synced by chrony. It will create a new sandbox 0b4c9da99f482 with timestamp _**2023-11-21T13:57:27.095899765-07:00**_
```
aff8aea34f502       4 weeks ago         NotReady            x-generic22-kdw2k                        sdprod              0                   (default)
0b4c9da99f482       10 months ago       Ready            x-generic22-kdw2k                    sdprod             1                   (default)
```
4. After the time is synced by chrony, kubelet will re-create the sandbox because the ready sandbox is not the latest one. The latest one is aff8aea34f502. The attempt is 0. So kubelet will use attempt +1 = 1 as the new attempt. but creating sandbox will fail. 
```
aff8aea34f502       4 weeks ago         NotReady            x-generic22-kdw2k                        sdprod              0                   (default)
0b4c9da99f482       10 months ago       NotReady            x-generic22-kdw2k                    sdprod             1                   (default)
```


https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/util/util.go#L42

```
func PodSandboxChanged(pod *v1.Pod, podStatus *kubecontainer.PodStatus) (bool, uint32, string) {
...
// Needs to create a new sandbox when readySandboxCount > 1 or the ready sandbox is not the latest one.
	sandboxStatus := podStatus.SandboxStatuses[0]
	if readySandboxCount > 1 {
		klog.V(2).InfoS("Multiple sandboxes are ready for Pod. Need to reconcile them", "pod", klog.KObj(pod))
```

title: Slow FSGroup recursive permission changes cause customer confusion
body:
### What happened?

[FSGroup volume permission setting](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/security-context/#configure-volume-permission-and-ownership-change-policy-for-pods) is very useful for making NFS volumes just work in spite of the impedance between containers and traditional user id based linux file permissions. 

However, in practice with large volumes, fsgroup settings can cause workloads to effectively get stuck, as it can take hours or days to recursively change permissions on multi-terabyte servers. The fsGroupChangePolicy has helped that (onRootMismatch is a win), but this has still been a perennial source of customer issues.

The [kubelet does log when a long fsgroup change is in progress](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/volume/volume_linux.go#L49), but this does not provide enough actionable information.


### What did you expect to happen?


The kubelet logging could be extended to provide updates of long-running fsgroup recursion, and maybe even some kind of progress (eg, some estimates of how much of the file tree has been walked).

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reproduction requires a large volume with many files, but it can be done with any volume type, eg RWO.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

All versions

In the implementation i have used `info.IsDir()` to determine if the current item is a directory or not. The `fileCount` and `dirCount` variables keep track of the total files and directories processed.
And then we are periodically logging to provide the progress updates every 1000 items processed or every 10 seconds.
Would like to hear from other members also if we have some better way to implement this.
Are you also planning to send periodically events as well similar to the previous attempt in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119359?

The implementation in the `volume_linux.go` file in the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119359/files) is conceptually the same. but there are some differences in the implementation of the solution.

Like my code, it executes the recursive traversal synchronously and logs progress based on processed file counts or time intervals. while the code in the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119359/files) runs the recursive operation in a separate goroutine and uses a ticker to log periodic warnings.

Another difference is that my code tracks and logs the number of files and directories processed at regular intervals while the code in the [PR](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/119359/files) focuses on issuing warnings periodically if the operation takes too long.

Any reason you prefer to do it synchronously instead of in a separate goroutine? A separate goroutine can have better performance and does not block the main application, but it may concurrent access files etc.

I think I like your idea of counting the files and updating progress from within the goroutine. I think that we do have to emit an event and not just a log -- not sure if that works from inside the goroutine, but you could always pass events out on a channel if it doesn't.

Feedback from the sig-storage meeting, 1000 maybe too little, 10 seconds maybe too frequent. Because for filesystem the whole process can take 30mins etc. Maybe 1-3 mins is more appropriate. Time maybe more important than the number of files.

If we have existing metrics to indicate how long this takes to verify.

Maybe we do the following as a start.
```
if time.Since(startTime).Seconds() > 60 {
  klog.V(2).Infof("FSGroup permission change in progress for %s: %d files, %d directories processed", dir, fileCount, dirCount)
  startTime = time.Now() // Reset timer for the next interval
}
```

> A separate goroutine can have better performance and does not block the main application, but it may concurrent access files etc.

I agree. 



> Any reason you prefer to do it synchronously instead of in a separate goroutine?

The primary reason for preferring synchronous execution is to avoids concurrency issues, as concurrent access to the same files or directories could lead to race conditions or inconsistencies.

> I think I like your idea of counting the files and updating progress from within the goroutine. I think that we do have to emit an event and not just a log -- not sure if that works from inside the goroutine, but you could always pass events out on a channel if it doesn't.

I agree that using a goroutine and emitting progress updates from within it can improve performance and responsiveness. 

I'll update the implementation to utilize a separate goroutine for file processing while sending progress updates and events through a channel.
